en: Second Chapter:
In a king who is exceedingly deep, like a well from which people cannot descend, virtuous intermediaries bring about the accomplishment of one's desired ends. (2.1)
The day deposits upon the impassioned lotus the splendor born of the sun;
for the virtuous, altruism—regardless of merits or faults—is a natural inclination.

Then, there were [the hermitages], resonant with the sound of unceasing Vedic recitation; inhabited by young students who, with foreheads made pale by marks of sacred ash and heads matted with masses of tawny locks, resembled fires arrived out of greed for sacrificial offerings; and whose courtyards were turning green with small plots of *soma* plants tender from constant watering.
There were parched *śyāmāka* grains for the sacrificial cakes scattered upon black antelope skins;
there were offerings of wild rice being strewn by young girls; and there were bundles of green *kuśa* grass and *palāśa* wood being brought by hundreds of pure disciples to serve as fuel.
The courtyards were crowded with piles of fuel and lumps of clay;
their thresholds were scarred by the circles of hooves of the *agnihotra* cows that yielded milk for the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*);
and the ascetics there were busily engaged in kneading lumps of clay for water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*).

Its borders were purified by heaps of branches from *udumbara* trees used as sacrificial pegs for the Vedic altars; its grounds were whitened by the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) offered to the Viśvedevas; the sprouts of the trees in its courtyards were turned grey by the smoke of oblations; and its calves were made to prance playfully by the young boys of the Vatsa clan.

Delighting as he wandered through the houses of his long-absent kinsmen— which displayed a continuous succession of animal sacrifices manifested by playful young black antelopes and goats, and which offered the pleasure of rest to their preceptors through the recitations commenced by parrots and mainas— he felt as if he were entering the very groves of the triple Vedas in person.
Bāṇa lived there in comfort.

While he was residing there, one day, the Great Time (Mahākāla) known as Summer yawned, withdrawing the pair of eras belonging to the season of flowers; its loud laughter was the white blossoms of the full-blown jasmine.
Having recently conquered and driven away the neighboring Vernal King, it showed affection toward the new gardens—which were like young children drinking milk—becoming gentle toward them.
And the scorching summer season, newly arisen, brought about the loosening of the bonds of all flowers upon the entire earth.
The masses of hair on the heads of amorous women were seized by the Flower-Armed God (Kāma) like bundles of yak-tail whisks moistened by the coronation of the King of Seasons himself.
And the sun, as if in anger at the destruction of all lotus ponds by the frost, set out on a journey toward the Himalayas.

Then, as the sun blazed, scorching the forehead, the women—wearing sectarian marks (*puṇḍraka*) of sandalwood paste upon their foreheads, draped in the rags of their tresses as garments, and bearing rosaries of pearl-like beads of perspiration—seemed to undertake religious observances for the propitiation of the Sun.

With their moon-like splendor on their foreheads, they were perceived as if by the light of the lunar crescent. Pale with sandalwood paste and unable to endure the sight of the sun, the beautiful women slept during the day like night-blooming lilies (*kumudinī*).
Drowsy with sleep, their eyes could not endure even the light of jewels, much less the harsh glare of the sun;
the nights, accompanied by the moon, were reduced to thinness like rivers that have grown slender during the non-cold season and are celebrated by pairs of cakravāka birds.

Due to the heat of the sun, people longed not only for water, but even for the wind, which was fragrant with the fresh, sharp scent of *pāṭala* flowers; and gradually, as the harsh rays of the sun shattered their childhood, [the day advanced].
In a lake that was drying up, in a river that was sinking, and in a sluggish waterfall resounding with the chirping of crickets;
The entire world was deafened by the continuous cooing of terrified doves;
the birds were gasping for breath, and the wind was harsh against the withered ears of grain.
In the spreading creepers,
where young lion cubs, curious about blood, were licking the hard clusters of dhātakī flowers;
and where the slopes of the great mountain were quivering from the crushing of a troop of elephants in distress.
When the bees were rendered silent as they clung to the dark, drying ichor of elephants tormented by the sun;
when the boundaries were reddened by the vermilion of the blooming Mandāra flowers;
and when the crystal rocks were being scratched and split by the tips of the horns of great buffaloes, who were bewildered by the suspicion that they were masses of trickling water.
In the heat where the earth crackles with parching warmth,
where the birds are terrified by the beds of hot sand,
and where the porcupines seek refuge in their burrows;

When the waters of the ponds were reduced to mere mud-speckled remnants, with minnows tossing on their backs from the feverish agitation caused by the warbling of shore-dwelling *arjuna* and *kurara* birds;
when the world was being consecrated by the forest fire as if for a royal lustration; and when the night was afflicted by consumption.
In the season of summer, as it grows harsh, there appear in every direction plunderers manifesting from the thatched roofs of water-sheds on saline wastes;
they drag across the gravelly, stony tracts— itchy with the irritation of dry grass— as if itching their ears with the restless flicking of clusters of ripe *kapikacchu* seeds,
scattering fine dust from large stones.

Roughened by the bursting forth of *mucukunda* buds, their bodies cooled by the spray from the mouths of flocks of *cīrī* birds chirping under the continuous heat of the sun, they seemed to be swimming in the false waters of mirage-rivers, shimmering under the intense heat of the young sun.

With legs swift and light in leaping over paths resounding with the crackling of parched *śamī* wood; acting as actors in a fierce dance (*ārabhaṭī*) whose frantic rhythm was the forceful clearing of circles of dust-eddies;
soiled by contact with the soot of forest lands scorched by wildfires; and gathering heaps of peacock feathers from the woods like monks practicing the conduct of mendicants.

They were like those ready for departure with the clusters of seeds from the rustling, aging *karañja* blossoms; they seemed full of longing through the thick sighs from the nostrils of forest buffaloes distressed by the heat;
they appeared to have offspring in the flocks of swift wind-hares leaping up;
and they were as if frowning with the curved tips of smoke rising from the heaps of chaff burning in the threshing floors.
It was as if possessed of the Avīci hell’s waves through its emissions of great heat;
as if covered in hair by the cotton-fibers of withering Śālmalī fruits;
and as if afflicted with leprosy by the dragging of heaps of dry leaves.

They were like those with prominent veins due to their tossing of grassy creepers; they were like those with long beards due to the whirling spikes of fresh grain-awn fragments; they were like those with fangs due to hundreds of moving *śalala* thorns;
and they were like those with tongues due to the flames of fire.

With their sloughing skins rising up like Cūḍālā, as it were, making a practice of seizing mouthfuls of warm honey from the lotus groves for the purpose of devouring the essence of the cosmic pillar (brahmastamba); and manifesting a terror of the three worlds with the sharp sounds of cracking dry bamboo forests— sounds that served like the dreadful drums of proclamation for the heat that dries up all waters.
Their paths were streaked by rows of the wings of partridges fluttering as they fled;
their bodies appeared as if variegated by the scorching of the forest of its own rays of light, marked on their limbs with sparks and embers like bursting gunja berries;
and their movements were terrifying due to deep, echoing roars from mountain caves.

Skilled in the sacrificial cooking of malevolent rites for the reduction of the world to ashes, they gratified the forest fires with showers of *pāribhadra* tree clusters as if with offerings of blood; their speed was such that it caused the hot sands to sparkle like stars.

The intoxicated winds began to blow, coating the quarters with the liquid essence of bitumen melting from heated rocks, and pungent with the scent of the steaming masses of insects within tree hollows— hollows filled with fragments of sparrow eggs being cooked by forest fires.
And on all sides, there were winds blowing from the deep throat-cavities of aged pythons, as if agitated by the fanning of thousands of great bellows;
here, deer wandered freely among the grass, and there,
mongooses rolled in the hollows at the foot of trees.
In one place were tawny matted locks hanging down; in another, hawks swooping down upon the nests of flocks of birds;
in one spot, lips with a complexion reddened by dissolved lac-dye;
and elsewhere, arrows that had acquired swift flight from the feathers of captured birds.
In one place, they are extinguished, having completely burnt away the causes of rebirth;
in another, they are impassioned, fragrant with garments scented by flowers;
and elsewhere, they have dimmed luster, emitting clouds of smoke.
In some places they were like those who greedily devour the entire world, covered in ashes;
in some places they were extremely aged, with their bodies leaning against the tops of bamboo poles; and in some places they were like bitumen extracted from mountains.

In some places there were those who, though consuming all flavors, grew fat and wasted away; in others, fierce beings like burnt guggulu resin; and in yet others, those who, having established their abodes upon the motionless Śiva, had burned the flower-arrowed Madana with the fire of their blazing eyes.

In some places, these actors of the violent dance (*ārabhaṭī*) with their flickering crests began a performance, as if worshipping the sun with handfuls of flames from the dried beds of lakes— flames that scattered parched grain-like seeds of withered *nīvāra* grass—
as they greedily consumed the stench of the fat of hard-shelled tortoises being forcibly offered by those devoid of pity;
and in the thickets, they seemed to devour even their own smoke for fear of the birth of clouds, while offering oblations of sesame seeds in the form of swarms of bursting young insects.
In the dried-up lakes, there were conch-shells and oysters white with bark that had burst open from the heat, resembling lepers;
and in the forests, there were showers of beeswax dripping from globes of honeycombs as swarms of bees dissolved away, resembling those afflicted with perspiration.

Terrible forest fires were seen: their masses of crests scattering like chaff upon great salt-wastes, and appearing as if they had seized mouthfuls of stone upon mountains where fragments of sun-stones were blazing.

And while he was thus situated in his own home, having finished his meal during the afternoon of one such exceedingly fierce summer season, his brother Candrasena— a son of a Śūdra woman— entered and said: "This [man] indeed belongs to Your Majesty, the sovereign of the four oceans, whose toe-nails are polished by the friction of the tips of the crest-jewels in the rows of the entire circle of kings."

"A most distinguished long-distance traveler, sent by your brother named Kṛṣṇa— the leader of all universal monarchs, the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord Śrī Harṣadeva— waits at the gate to see you.
He replied, "Long-lived one!"
"Bring him in without delay. Then, as he was being led forward, his shanks appeared heavy and sluggish from the great distance he had traveled.
His coarse outer garment was tightly bound by a strip of cloth from a dyer’s shop; a knot was tied at his neck with a ragged piece of tattered raiment dangling behind him;
and his head was encircled by a garland of parched grain, the gaps between its rows being clearly defined by the deep indentations made by the binding of very thick threads.
He saw a letter-carrier entering and questioned him from afar: "Good man,
is all well with the venerable Kṛṣṇa, who is the disinterested friend of the entire world?"
Saying "It is well," he bowed and sat down not far away.
Once rested, he said, "Indeed, this letter has been sent by my lord for one worthy of honor. Having said this, he unsealed and handed it over.

Bāṇa, however, took it with respect and read it himself: "Having understood the message from Mekhalaka, a wise man must avoid delay, which obstructs the attainment of results; such is the substance of the matter here."
The other was merely a matter of exchanging news. Having ascertained the meaning of the letter and having dismissed his attendants, he asked for the message.
Mekhalaka replied: "My lord says thus to the wise one: 'The honorable sir surely knows that, whether by virtue of belonging to the same lineage, or...'"
Whether it be equality of knowledge, equality of birth,
or having grown up together;
Dwelling in the same place, the practice of seeing one another, or mutual affection;
Whether it be hearing [the Dharma],
performing beneficial acts in one's absence, or sharing a common character;
These are the causes of affection.

But in your case, though no cause is perceived and you are unseen, my heart feels an inexplicable attachment as if toward a kinsman standing nearby; even though you are far away, it loves you just as a bed of night-lotuses loves the moon.
For, without you, this universal monarch was led astray by wicked men in various ways.
And yet, that is not so; for there are no such beings among those who exist for whom friends, neutrals, and enemies do not exist.
Furthermore, because your mental disposition was turned away from childish fickleness, something unsuitable was uttered by someone intolerant;
and the rest of the world perceives and speaks of it exactly as it is.
The minds of the undiscerning are indeed as fickle as water, following whatever path it encounters;

what can a lord of the earth do when his resolve has been unsettled by hearing various accounts from many sources? And though you remain at a distance, you have been made manifest to us who seek the truth.
The Cakravartin has been informed on your behalf that, generally speaking, childhood offends through the restlessness of all beings in their first stage of life.
And the Lord has agreed, saying, "So be it.
Therefore, you should come without causing any delay to the royal camp.

One who is barren of devotion and has not beheld the Supreme Lord is not highly regarded by me, even if he dwells in the midst of kinsmen. Nor should you be one who is dejected by the hardships of service, or one who fears approaching the Supreme Lord;
for although He does not grant his own will-born objects even when they are sought with hundreds of petitions, and though He bestows suffering—
Out of delusion, he suddenly snatches away even life, like the wicked-minded god of love who forcibly drags one away.
Nevertheless, those other kings were one thing,
while this lord is quite another; he is a master composed of nectar, who has surpassed Nṛga, Nala, Niṣadha, Nahuṣa, Ambarīṣa, Daśaratha, Dilīpa, Nābhāga, Bharata, Bhagīratha, Yayāti, and Rama.

His glances were not defiled by the poison of the *kālakūṭa* of ego; his speech was not faltering with the heavy seizure of the venom of pride; and his postures did not forget their steadfastness due to the epilepsy of the heat of excessive arrogance.

There were no physical distortions caused by the agitation of the feverish force of unrestrained pride; there were no faltering steps produced by the great derangement of arrogance; nor were there any harsh words spat out with lips curled from the affliction of intoxication.
And so it is: his perception of them as jewels is directed toward pure saints, not toward fragments of stone;
his mind for adornment is fixed upon virtues white as pearls.
He has faith in the means for performing acts of giving, not in the burden of ornaments; he has faith in elephants,
not in insects.
He felt great joy in his fame, which was foremost among all things, but not in his life, which was like withered grass;
he applied himself to accomplishing his goals toward the quarters of the sky that had grasped his hand, but not toward his own wife or daughters-in-law.
He regards the bow as his companion because it possesses virtues,
not the retinue of servants who subsist on his alms;
moreover, his very self is the instrument for his friend's service.
Mastery is the means for servants;
cleverness is the means for scholars;
and fortune is the means for kinsmen.
Sovereignty was a means for assisting the wretched; his entire fortune was a means for assisting the twice-born;
and his heart was a means for recollecting his good deeds.
The equipment for dharma was his life; the equipment for daring was his body; the equipment for the sword was the earth;
and the equipment for diversion was the royal court.
"An adversary is the instrument of one's majesty;
the shade of the foliage of this tree, which produces the essence of a bliss surpassing all else, cannot be attained by those of meager merit.
Having heard this, he commanded that very Candrasena: "Provide him with food and let him rest in comfort."
Then, after he had departed and the day had declined,
as the afternoon sunlight— reddened like the beak of a young crow— became thin and faded, being drunk up as it were by the closing calyxes of the gathering red lotuses;

When the sun, its own speed slackened, had stumbled upon the peaks of the western mountains which were as red as a cluster of hibiscus flowers, and was limping as if its tender feet were wounded by the thorns of the lotus plants; and when the face of night, dark as if from the grief of separation from the moon, approached with its dangling locks of flickering fragments of darkness, he performed his evening devotions and retired to his bed.
And he thought to himself alone: "What shall I do? I have been treated differently by the king, and Kṛṣṇa, that friend without cause, has sent me this very message."
Service is arduous; the condition of a servant is precarious;
and the great royal court is exceedingly profound.
Nor was it because of any affection for my ancestors established there, nor because of a path inherited through family lineage, nor out of a sense of obligation to remember past favors.
There was no affection born of serving fools, no pride of lineage,
and no courtesy resulting from past acquaintance.
There was no seduction by the distribution of wisdom, no curiosity regarding superior knowledge,
and no regard for the beauty of outward form.
There was no skill in the gestures of service,
no cleverness in joining the assemblies of the learned,
and no mastery over the expenditure of wealth.
I have no acquaintance with the king’s favorites,
and I must certainly depart.
In every way, the Blessed Lord Bhavānīpati, the Protector of the World, is my refuge once I have gone.
"Thinking, 'He will perform everything appropriately,' he resolved to depart;
then, on another day, having risen,"
Having bathed early in the morning,
wearing white silk garments and holding a rosary of beads, he—

Having repeatedly recited the hymns and mantra-words appropriate for departure, and having performed with supreme devotion a worship of the God of gods, Virūpākṣa, preceded by a ceremonial bath with milk and abounding in fragrant flowers, incense, perfumes, banners, offerings, ointments, and many lamps;

Having offered oblations into the venerable fire— the crest of whose flickering tongues was made restless by the cracking of the skin of the freshly poured ghee-libations, and whose southern flame was intensified by abundant offerings of clarified butter—
and having bestowed wealth upon the twice-born according to his means,
she circumambulated the black cow facing the east.
With white unguents on his body,
white garlands,
and white garments.
He had fashioned ear-ornaments from *rocanā*, variegated *dūrvā* grass, young sprouts, and *girikarṇikā* flowers;

he wore white mustard seeds bound in his topknot; and all the auspicious rites for his departure had been performed by his father’s younger sister named Mālatī, whose heart was moist with affection like that of a mother, who wore white garments and appeared like the goddess Mahāśvetā in person.
He was granted blessings by the elderly female relatives,
congratulated by the aged women of the household, permitted to depart by his gurus who saluted his feet,
and had his head smelled by the family elders who offered him their greetings.
His enthusiasm for the journey increased by the omens of the birds;
having fulfilled the ritual longing for the lunar mansion according to the opinion of the astrologers,
at an auspicious moment he placed the sacrificial post— encircled with garlands of flowers other than black— upon a leveled altar in the courtyard smeared with fresh cow dung.

Beholding a full water-jar white with five-finger marks of applied flour and a fresh mango sprout placed upon its mouth, he bowed to his family deities and, followed by his own brahmins who carried flowers and fruits in their hands and were chanting the *Apratiratha* hymn,
he took his first step with his right foot.
He emerged from Prītikūṭa.

On that first day, however, he beheld the Ghaṭotkaca mountain—oppressed by the heat of summer, devoid of water, made uneven by leafless trees, and where the footprints of entering travelers were worshipped with offerings to the image of Kātyāyanī carved upon its base;

though parched, it seemed as if it had sprouted new leaves through the thousands of trembling tongues of thirsty beasts of prey lolling out, and it seemed to bristle with joy through the swarms of bees agitated by honey-clots being licked by bears and monkeys.
With the hundreds of thick *abhīru* sprouts growing on the scorched ground appearing as if his hair were standing on end,
he gradually passed through the forest of Caṇḍikā’s temple and reached a village named Mallakūṭa.
There, having been provided with hospitality by his brother and friend named Jagatpati, who was no different from his own heart, he dwelt in comfort.
Then, on the following day, having crossed the blessed Bhāgīrathī, he spent the night in a forest village named Yaṣṭigṛhaka.
On another day, he reached the royal camp established at Anvajiravatī near the city of Upamaṇipura,
and he stayed not far from the king’s palace.
Having completed his bathing and eating, and having rested with Mekhalaka, he proceeded slowly as the day had only one watch remaining, while the king had already eaten;
observing the many encampments of renowned monarchs,
he saw those [elephants] brought forward for the binding of their frontal fillets, those led up for the mounting of the war-drums, those newly captured, and those acquired through plunder.

And with those arriving as auspicious greetings, those brought by curiosity at their first sight, those sent by the guardians of the Naga-pathways, those presented by the chiefs of the forest hamlets,

those summoned out of a desire for the sport of voluntary combat, and those dispatched by the sending of messengers— being given, being intercepted, being released, and being stationed for the watches— he, desiring to conquer all the continents, appeared like mountains gathered together for the purpose of building a bridge across the ocean, made beautiful by banners, fluttering drums, conchs, chowries, and body-unguents.
The city was darkened by lordly elephants, as if they were the very days of the Puṣya-consecration;
they seemed to make the Goddess of Royal Fortune dance with the drums struck by their incessantly moving hooves,

to mock her with the loud laughter of foam issuing from the corners of their mouths, to summon the race of deer whose legs were paralyzed by speed, and to leap high toward Uccaiḥśravas for the sake of a collision, with their joyful neighing.
The sky was made to ripple by horses that appeared like Yakṣas through their rows of decorative chowries, as if out of anger toward the steeds of the sun’s chariot;

they were adorned with rows of cowrie shells— used for counting the number of leagues traveled, those currently being sent, those already dispatched, and those returning from their missions— which seemed like clusters of stars or fragments of twilight glow, with crimson chowries fashioned into ear-ornaments.
It was turning tawny with herds of camels,

as brown as the cheeks of monkeys, resembling groves of red rice with their fields of red *śāli* paddy, appearing like forests of *karañja* trees with their hundreds of rustling, dry seed-pods, and possessing masses of matted hair formed by bundles of variegated threads of five-colored wool that dangled near their ears.

There, with bodies white as masses of water freshly shed by autumnal clouds, they were like *kalpavṛkṣa* trees whose circles of shade were stolen by the light emanating from clusters of pearls; like the lotuses from the navel of Nārāyaṇa embraced by the wings of Garuḍa;
like regions of the Ocean of Milk with their massive coral stalks shining brightly; and like the broad plates of Śeṣa’s hoods with large rubies flashing upon them.

[The lakes] were like the white sands of the Gaṅgā, frequented by royal swans; they seemed to overwhelm the summer season, to mock the majesty of the sun, and to drink up the heat; they made the world of living beings appear as if it were the realm of the moon, turned time into one consisting of white water-lilies, fashioned the day into moonlight, showed the sky to be composed of foam, and released thousands of untimely blossoms of the night-lily, as if in derision.
With its white parasol-canopies shining like Śvetadvīpa, it possessed the splendor of Indra; and with those [parasols] which,

appearing and vanishing in every direction in an instant, seemed to rob the world of its light, making the day appear as if tossed on a swing by their coming and going, and as if driving away the Kali-age condition blackened by the stain of contact with wicked kings.

With thousands of waving chowries, white as the petals of a blooming *kāśa* forest, making the ten directions pale like the autumn season and revealing the sky as if it were woven from lotus fibers, the palace was shimmering;
moreover, the elephant-ear-fans resembled a flock of swans.
It resembled a grove of wish-fulfilling creepers because of its plantain trees; it resembled a forest of ruby-trees because of its peacock-umbrellas;
and it resembled the flow of the Mandākinī river because of its silken garments.
It appeared like the Ocean of Milk through its silken garments,
like a grove of plantain trees through the rays of emerald, and like a second day being created by the morning sunlight of the red lotuses.
It was as if a second sky were being produced by masses of sapphire light;

as if a new night were being commenced by the darkness of great sapphire rays; as if thousands of flowing Yamunās were being poured forth by the expansions of emerald luster; it was as if covered in glowing coals by the beams of topaz, while certain rays, finding no entrance, seemed to fall headlong with their reflections from the face onto the toenails, as if out of shame.
Some, as if entering his very limbs, seemed to offer chowries of service under the guise of the clusters of rays from their fingernails as they scratched the earth;

others, with the flickering bands of sapphire light swaying upon their chests, appeared as if they had bound swords around their necks to appease their master’s anger; and others, whose faces were darkened by swarms of bees circling the fragrance of their breath, seemed to have grown long beards out of grief for having been robbed of Fortune.

The attendants following those inner doorkeepers— who emerged and re-entered at intervals, their crowns seemingly fleeing in fear of the mockery of prostration by swarms of bees hovering over their crests as if they had been conquered yet highly honored, and who were followed by thousands of supplicants led along the path—
were questioned again and again by tireless men asking, "O good sir!"

It was attended on all sides by great feudatories of his enemies, subdued by the strength of his arms, who spent the day with the hope of a vision, thinking, "Today the Supreme Lord, having eaten, will grant an audience in this place," or "He will emerge onto the outer terrace";
and it was occupied by other great provincial lords from various lands, arrived out of devotion to his majesty, who waited for the time of the king's appearance.
He was attended by Jains, Ārhatas, Pāśupatas, and followers of Pārāśarya seated in solitude; by forest-dwellers (varṇins) and people born in every land;

by Mleccha tribes dwelling on the forested shores of all the oceans; and by circles of envoys arrived from every other country—appearing like the very ground for the creation of all subjects by the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis).
It was as if a fourth world fashioned from the accumulated essence of the three worlds;
its abundance of prosperity could not be described even by hundreds of *Mahābhāratas*;
its layout seemed designed by thousands of *Kṛta* ages; and its loveliness surpassed that of millions of celestial realms.
He went to the palace gate, which was as if occupied by millions of royal fortunes.

And a sense of wonder arose in his mind: "How could there have been no exhaustion for the creators of beings who produced this vast multitude of living creatures, or was there perhaps an exhaustion of the great elements?"
Or the disintegration of atoms,
or the end of time,
or the cessation of life.
"Or rather, it is the completion of the forms.

But Mekhalaka, recognized from afar by the gatekeeper, said to him, "Wait here for just a moment, you fortunate one," and entered unimpeded into the presence. Then, after what seemed like a mere moment, he [saw] a tall man...
With a body as fair as the *karṇikāra* flower,
his form covered by a fine silken tunic,
and his slender waist adorned with a beautiful girdle-string bound with a row of shimmering rubies;
With a chest as broad as a slab of the snowy mountain,
with shoulders as rugged as the hump of Shiva’s bull,
and wearing upon his breast a necklace that resembled a snare for binding the flock of restless deer that are the senses;

"Tell me, has there ever been a king such as this, born of the Lunar dynasty or the Solar dynasty?"— thus he greeted them from afar with a long gaze that brought joy, as if they were the Moon and the Sun themselves brought before his ears to be questioned; a gaze that seemed to draw forth the very stream of the beauty flowing from his face, which, due to the gravity of their office, was being surrendered by the rays of the Sun as if out of deference, and which appeared like a garland of full-blown white lotuses obtained through his favor.
Although he stood upon a foundation of sternness, at every step he seemed to bow with humility; wearing a white turban upon his head,
he carried a sword in his left sprout-like hand, its hilt bristling with an inlay of large pearls.

Followed by a man carrying a polished golden cane— its flickeringness removed by another person, like a lightning-flash or a reed-staff— he emerged and said: "This indeed is the gatekeeper named Pāriyātra, who stands immediately after the great chamberlains and is dear to the sight of His Majesty."
“May he favor him with a corresponding practice, for he is intent upon what is wholesome.
Then the doorkeeper, having approached and offered his salutation, spoke with humility in a sweet voice: “Come!
Enter to behold the King.”
"The King has shown his favor," [said the attendant].
Bāṇa, however, replied, "I am blessed that the King deems me worthy of such grace," and, with the path being pointed out by him, he entered the inner apartments.
Then, with horses born in Vanāyu, those born in Āraṭṭa, and those of the Bhāradvāja breed.
By those born in the land of Sindhu,
by the Persians, and by the Śoṇas;
And with those that are dark, white, and tawny;
And with those marked by yellow,
those variegated like partridges,
and those possessing the five auspicious marks.
And those with eyes like jasmine flowers,
tawny as the Kṛttikās,
and with faces devoid of flesh.
with ear-holes that were not protruding;
with throat-bands that were well-rounded, smooth, and well-fitted; and with necks that were curved, long, and upward-pointing like sacrificial posts.
With the joints of their hooves thickened by constant breathing,

with chests arched upward, and with circular hooves as hard as iron pedestals— straight, stout, and extended— they bore rounded bellies that seemed as if they had no intestines, fearing they might burst from excessive distension.
With their broad hips revealed as their girdles rose up,
with young shoots dangling like swings upon the earth,
they were somehow restrained by being bound on both sides with firm, thick ropes fastened to stakes driven into the ground.
With one leg stretched out, rendered helpless by the binding of the tether behind them so that they appeared as if even longer, their neck-bells strung together with cords of many threads,
and their eyes closed.

with their hindquarters—dappled with fragments of foam dark as the juice of *dūrvā* grass—being scratched by those who had seized and released them with their teeth, causing the skin to quiver; with their tails swaying languidly; and with the lower halves of their bodies drooping and slackened from the fatigue of resting upon their single hooves.
Some were lost in thought due to sleep; others were emitting faint, stumbling sounds of "huṃ";
some were longing for fodder, their hooves striking the earth and their manes bristling as they scratched the ground with their tips, making it resonant with their cries.
With their hooves striking the earth, making the tips of their manes resonant as they scratched the ground, and longing for fodder;
agitated by the greed arising from their desire for mouthfuls of scattered grass;
and with pupils trembling with extreme fear at the angry roars of fierce outcastes.

Beholding the stable, which was adorned with horses dear to the king— horses whose bodies were tawny from being rubbed with saffron as if they were being constantly protected by the fires of the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) held near them, and beneath which canopies were spread out, while their favorite deities were worshipped before them.

With his heart captivated by curiosity, having traversed some distance, he beheld from afar the indistinct temple of the elephant-god (Gaṇeśa), which, on its left side, seemed to leave no room for the sky due to its extreme height; its perimeter was surrounded by a vast grove of plantain trees, and it was being filled on all sides by streams of rut flowing like rivers composed of swarms of bees; and it appeared to anoint the sense of smell with the fragrance of blossoming *bakula* groves spreading toward the quarters of the horizon.
And he asked, "What is Your Majesty doing here?

He replied, "This is indeed the great pavilion where the lord of elephants resides—the elephant that serves Your Majesty as a mount, his very heart externalized, his soul incarnated in another birth, his outward-moving vital breaths, his friend in the sport of valor, and the shatterer of pride; thus, he is truly named Vāraṇapati."
He said to him: "Good sir, it is heard that Darpaśāta is here; if this is so, or if there is no fault, I would like to see that very lord of elephants for a moment.
Therefore, you ought to lead me there."
"I am exceedingly eager with curiosity," he said.
He replied, "Let it be so;
please come."
"What is the harm?
Let him see the lordly elephant first.

Having gone to that place, even from afar he beheld [the elephant] surrounded by flocks of *cātaka* birds in the sky and by throngs of domestic peacocks on the ground, their faces resonant with the tumultuous, sweet-sounding cries of their keketas.
Filling the world with the fragrance of rut-fluid that rivaled the scent of blooming *kadamba* flowers;
appearing like the untimely monsoon season incarnate;
and casting off the fourth stage of life—which was like plunging into a lake overgrown with a dense network of lotuses tawny with dripping drops of honey.
He seemed to announce the auspicious commencement of an entry into the fifth musical note with the incessant, deep-sounding drums of his flapping ears that resembled ear-ornaments;

with the graceful rhythm of his dancing on his variegated, ever-moving three-hoofed feet, he appeared to lighten his burden— his long, expansive body swaying like a swing— as if out of fear of splitting the earth,
or as if scratching his own body against the slopes of the walls of the quarters.
With his trunk raised for battle, he seemed to be summoning the elephants of the quarters;
with his thick, sharp tusk acting as a saw, he appeared to be cleaving the world-stalk asunder;
and being unable to fit within the interior of the universe, he seemed to desire to go outside.
It was as if scattered by forests where bees hovered over creepers with blossoms fresh on every side, long accustomed to them;

and it afforded the joy of treatments appropriate to the summer season being administered by mahouts through lakes whose waters were mottled with masses of moss and lotus stalks. Moreover, its exceedingly massive belly was rippled with thin lines of wrinkles—like rows of scars counting his victories in many battles—which had been tossed far upward by the wind from the ichor of rival elephants.
He seemed to be barring the entire circle of the quarters— along with its mountains, oceans, islands, and forests— with the staff-like bolt of his hand;
he bore one lotus-stalk held between his fingers with its root being sprinkled by internal spray,
while the other, dangling playfully, was like a sprouting leaf, making his ivory tusks appear as if bristling with horripilation from the thrill of the passion for battle.
With the luster of his pair of tusks spreading forth, he seemed to be vomiting out in many ways the beds of night-lotuses tasted during his sports in the lakes;
he appeared to be bestowing upon the quarters of the sky the mass of his own fame,
and was mocking lions as if they were mere cockroaches rendered arrogant by their skill in tearing apart small insects.
He seemed to fashion for himself a face-cloth of fine silk from the wish-fulfilling tree;
and as he sportively raised his staff-like forearm, he appeared to rain down groves of red lotuses— swallowed by his palate, which was more delicate than crimson silk—
while simultaneously disgorging heaps of fresh sprouts.

With eyes naturally tawny, as if vomiting the sweet nectar they had drunk from the hollows of lotuses, he seemed to be offering up all the forests day and night under the guise of the thick fragrance of rut from his temples. These temples were adorned with ichor-bands that hummed with swarms of bees, scratched by the rubbing of half-chewed stalks of red sugarcane, and which— by their restless movements— appeared to have been repeatedly enjoyed like groves of *pārijātaka* trees mixed with mangoes, *campaka*, *lavalī*, cloves, *kakkola*, cardamom creepers, and nutmegs, and filled with camphor.
He was being cooled by a necklace of shimmering stars composed of fragments of moonstone that dripped incessant drops of water;
he bore his head very high, as if it were the auspicious binding of the turban of sovereignty over all the lords of elephants;

and, with his fan-like ears—like palm-leaf fans—that repeatedly covered and revealed the quarters of the sky, he seemed to be fanning the Goddess of Royal Fortune as she sat upon the couch of his tusks out of devotion to her lord.
He was resplendent with his tail, which moved like a fly-whisk—the insignia of lordship over elephants—descended through a long line of noble lineage;
he seemed to repeatedly discharge from his mouth, under the guise of clear and cool spray, the very rivers he had drunk during his conquest of the quarters;

and at the end of the contortions of his limbs caused by hearing the drums of other elephants, he made all his members motionless for a moment in attentive listening, as if announcing the pain of humiliation with long, hissing breaths.
Lamenting himself as if he had failed to obtain a battle,
appearing as if ashamed by the humiliation of being surpassed in mounting and riding, scratching the surface of the earth with his hooves, and shedding his rut-fluid.
With the third part of his eyes closed due to the drowsiness of rut, he was compelled by the braying of his mount, who was enraged by the morsels being taken and then released with contempt;
somehow, with great difficulty and indifferently, he was taking up the morsels,
while from his mouth he seemed to discharge a torrent of rutting-fluid in abundance, like the dark juice trickling from half-chewed *tamāla* sprouts.
As if quivering with pride,
as if panting with valor, and as if fainting with intoxication.
As if breaking asunder with youth,
as if flowing away with generosity,
as if leaping about with strength;
As if intoxicated by pride,
as if rising up with energy,
and as if fainting with splendor.
As if anointing with loveliness,
as if sprinkling with good fortune,
his nails were glossy.
He was harsh regarding his hair, severe toward his mouth,
and well-disciplined in his students.
Gentle on the head,
firm in the joints,
and short at the neck-binding.
Longevity,
a belly free from poverty, and the constant practice of giving.
Balabhadra in his playful intoxications, the family wife in her dependability, and the Jina in his forbearances.
Vahnivarṣa in the unleashing of wrath,
Garuḍa in the uprooting of serpents, and Nārada in the curiosity for quarrels.
A dry thunderbolt in sudden assaults,
a sea-monster in the churning of armies, and a venomous serpent in the act of biting.
Varuṇa in the drawing in of nooses for the hands, Yama in the entangling of enemies with snares,
and Kāla in the transformations of time.
Rāhu in the seizing of sharp rays, Mars in its retrograde motions,
and a circle of fire in the cognition of circular whirling.
It was the wish-fulfilling Cintāmaṇi mountain of valor;
the palace with its pillars of ivory and pearl-mountains where pride dwells;
and the celestial chariot for traveling at will, enchanting with its ornaments of bells and chowries, belonging to self-respect.
It was a shower-house for the water of perfumes, where the darkness of gloom was created by the downpour of ichor;
it was a great mansion for Egoism, adorned with golden statues;
and it was a pleasure-mountain for Arrogance, featuring cascades from its rocky peaks.
The diamond palace of Darpa had archways with six tusks;
the fortress of Rājya was formidable with its high water-jars, turrets, and watchtowers, like a movable mountain stronghold;
and the iron wall of Pṛthivī was pierced by thousands of openings for arrows.
The Pārijāta tree of the earthly paradise, resounding with the *jhāṅ* of hundreds of arrows; likewise, a concert hall for the rhythmic dances of his flapping ears,
and a drinking pavilion for the swarms of bees.
The inner apartments were the pinnacle of erotic ornaments;
the festival of passion was the dance of amorous playfulness; and the night was unbroken by the circles of star-garlanded necklaces.
An untimely monsoon season for the floods of the great rivers of intoxication; a false autumn for the fragrances of the saptacchada forests;
an unprecedented arrival of frost for the sprays of mist.
He beheld a false cloud, the pride of which was shattered by its own thunderous ostentation;
and it occurred to his mind: "Surely, in the creation of this [cloud], the mountains were reduced to the state of atoms."
"How else could such reverence exist?
This is marvelous! 'The tusks of the Vindhya; the trunk of the primordial boar!'—uttering this in astonishment, the doorkeeper spoke thus: 'Behold!'"

This lord of serpents, who had been painted by hundreds of desires as ever-present yet was utterly lost to those whose minds were distracted by the fabrication of means to recover their beloved, has somehow entered the path of memory for those whose hearts have become desolate; he cannot endure even the lordly elephants of hope that dwell within their minds.
"Come then; you shall see him again.
Just look at the King," he was told by him, as [the elephant] fell like one intoxicated, with its temples smeared with the mud of rut-fluid.
Having somehow drawn back his gaze, which had been closed by the fragrance of wine, and being shown the way by that very same doorkeeper,
he passed through three inner courtyards crowded with thousands of royal families and stood in the courtyard before the pearl-adorned pavilion of the assembly hall in the fourth.
At a distance stood his personal retinue of bodyguards—tall men, white as *karṇikāra* flowers, with bodies hardened by exercise and bearing weapons—arrayed in rows like a circle of golden pillars;
nearby sat his distinguished and beloved followers.

He himself was seated upon a couch made of a slab of pearl-stone, which seemed as if fashioned from the moon, with legs as white as ivory, its surface washed with liquid yellow sandalwood and cooled by sprays of frost.

With the entire weight of his body resting upon an arm placed at the edge of his bed, he was sporting with the circle of kings in a canopy of bodily radiance spreading toward the quarters of the sky, where the rays of jewels were diffused; it was like a lake in the season of summer, its waters entangled by a network of soft lotus stalks.
He appeared as if fashioned from the mere atoms of splendor.
The throne, as it were, forcibly compelled him to mount it even though he was unwilling;
he was embraced by all the auspicious marks in every limb, and having taken up the vow of celibacy, he was embraced by the Fortune of Kingship.

He was a royal sage who had undertaken the vow of wielding the edge of a sword and was free from contradiction; he was firmly established in dharma as if out of fear of tripping while placing his feet upon the uneven royal path;
and he was served with his whole soul by Truth, which had been abandoned by all other kings and had found its voice only in him, as if out of terror.

He was being saluted by the ten directions—personified as the reflections of the nearby courtesans falling upon his toe-nails—as if they were ten embodied goddesses who had abandoned their celestial forms;
with long glances reaching to the ends of the horizon, he seemed to be scrutinizing the deeds done and left undone by the world-protectors;
and with his hand resting upon the back of his jeweled footstool, he appeared to be seeking permission to ascend from the sun itself.
He was being circumambulated, as it were, by the day, which formed a circular boundary by dispersing the radiance of his ornaments;

he bore an immeasurable ocean of loveliness, white with sandalwood paste, which seemed to foam with the heat of his valor even while being tormented by mountains of immense size, through the singular majesty of his royal power.

He bore the Goddess of Royal Fortune, who, unable to endure even her own reflections held by the crest-jewels of the circle of kings, seemed to sigh repeatedly through the guise of the wind from the chowries as if out of the pain of jealous resentment;
he was embraced by Prosperity, who had arisen having taken up, as it were, the entire loveliness of the four oceans;

he seemed to be bestowing thousands of rainbows produced by the mass of rays from the jewels of his ornaments, as if they were presents sent by Indra; and in his conversations with kings, he showered honey, even though it had been abandoned.
He was one who, even while drinking from poetic tales, seemed to be vomiting forth nectar; who, even when his heart was not drawn away by confidential conversations, revealed its inner depths;
and who, in bestowing favors, established prosperity in every place, though it was already as steady as a mountain.
In the assemblies of heroes, he seemed to be hearing the secret messages of the Goddess of War with his hair-raising cheeks;

upon his beloved sword, he cast a glance that was like a shower of affection toward it after its talk with past warriors; and through the rays of his teeth, he seemed to declare the pure intentions of the assembly of kings, who were terrified by his great majesty, amidst their jesting smiles.
Though abiding in the hearts of all people, he remained established in justice;

he stood in a greatness that was beyond the range of virtues, outside the domain of good fortune, inaccessible to the granting of boons, impossible for blessings, a pathless track for desires, far beyond the reach of fate, and an unprecedented magnitude for prosperity, which cannot be accomplished by righteousness nor even perceived before.

With a body that displayed, as it were, the descent of all the gods into a single form— possessing dawn-red sprout-like feet, thighs as slow-moving as those of the Sugata, a forearm and back as firm as a thunderbolt-weapon, shoulders like a bull’s, lips like the radiant orb of the sun, a tranquil gaze, a moon-like face, and dark hair—

he rested his left foot with ease upon a great and precious footstool made of sapphire, its base adorned with a girdle of ruby strings and its surface darkened by a dense garland of rays, as if it were the very head of the Kali age.
He resembled the young Puṇḍarīkākṣa (Viṣṇu) as he trampled the circle of Kāliya’s hoods;
with the spreading expanse of light from his toenails, white as linen, he seemed to be bestowing greatness upon the earth by means of a royal turban for the Great Goddess.

His feet were exceedingly red, as if from the wrath of the world-protectors who had failed to bow before him, and they seemed to drink up the yellow luster of the ruby-gems in the garlands upon the crowns of all the kings.

They seemed to be wearing the twilight of the setting of all other radiant circles of kings; they appeared to be shedding streams of the sweet nectar from the flower-garlands on the heads of the remaining monarchs;

they were never for a moment separated from swarms of bees wandering about, drawn by the fragrance of the wreaths from the top-knots of all the feudatories, as if those bees were the heads of their enemies; and they resembled forest dwellings of blooming red lotuses for the Goddess of Fortune, who was intent upon her vehicle.
He bore two final [feet] that seemed to proclaim his enjoyment of the four oceans by having their soles adorned with lotuses, conchs, fish,
and sea-monsters; they were as beautiful as the tusks of the elephants of the quarters used to restrain fierce crocodile mouths,

possessed the splendor of foam from the overflowing currents of the ocean of loveliness, and had their bases illuminated by the rays of the crest-jewels of the circle of serpents, like two *kalā-candana* trees.
He was resplendent with two pillar-like thighs that served as ruby columns for supporting the weight of the earth placed upon his heart;

he shone like Mount Mandara encircled by the slough of Vāsuki, with a lower garment white as a mass of nectar-foam, studded with the rays of gems from his girdle, draped across his rounded hips, washed in pure water, and beautified by the fastening of its cord.
He appeared like the expanse of the world with a second sky formed above by a multitude of stars in the form of his spotless teeth;

he possessed a vast chest-plate as broad as the sky, hard and smooth from being rubbed by the thousands of pestles that were the tusks of lordly elephants, capable of enduring the tumultuous clamor and crush of various armies; it was marked by a line as if laid down to divide the enjoyment of the breasts and face of Śrī and Sarasvatī, and it bore a jeweled necklace like the serpent Śeṣa, who had fallen asleep in the bliss of rest after bearing the entire burden of the earth upon the pillar of his arm.

His neck was encircled by a mass of rays from the pearls of his necklace, which seemed like the initiation-garment for the great gift of surrendering all his possessions at the moment of his life’s end;

and his chest was covered by those rays as if by other infant arms, eager to conquer him, growing forth to serve as pillows for Śrī as she lay upon them, or like continuous streams of honey flowing from the lotuses on her ears.

With his pair of exceedingly long staff-like arms—which, like the paths for the exit of the majesty born of his own arms, were manifest with bracelets appearing like emerging rays of light; which resembled a canopy of jeweled wings spread on both sides;

which served as a bolt for the path of the Lokāloka mountain; which was a golden stone rampart dug out by the encircling moat of the four oceans; which was a diamond cage for the capture of all royal swans; and which was a great jeweled triumphal arch for the auspicious entry of the Fortune of the World—he [overawed] the quarters and the guardians of the quarters.
And he was simultaneously casting away his long strides;

with the crimson hue trickling from his lower lip—which had attained the status of a facial feature as if out of a longing to be kissed by its sister Lakṣmī, like the Kaustubha gem—he seemed to drench the faces of the quarters with the juice of Pārijāta sprouts;

and from time to time, by scattering the spreading rays of his pure white teeth through smiles of friendly jesting, he appeared to show the light of wisdom to the royal Fortune, who was otherwise naturally dull-witted.
He seemed to be sending away beds of night-lotuses that had approached him out of doubt that his face was the moon;

he appeared to be dismissing the autumnal moonlight that had entered his mouth under the suspicion that it was a bed of white water-lilies created by the rows of his teeth, which were as white as clear crystal;

and with the fragrance of his breath—which filled all the quarters of space with the scent of wine, nectar, and the *pārijāta* tree—he seemed to be recreating the very day of the churning of the ocean for the nectar.
He was incessantly inhaling the fragrance of his breath through the hollow of the pericarp of his blooming lotus-face with his downward-turned nose;
by the whiteness of his eyes, which were as oily as milk, he made the quarters of the sky appear as if flooded by an unprecedented ocean of milk surging from the rising moon of his countenance;
and he bore upon the surface of his spotless cheeks the image of the female fly-whisk bearer, who seemed like the goddess Sarasvatī herself, embodied and residing within his mouth.

His broad forehead was reddened by the glow of his crest-jewel, as if by the lac-dye from his feet clinging there to appease Lakṣmī, who had been angered by Sarasvatī; he listened to the warbling of the swarms of bees serving as ear-ornaments— bees that were like young lutes with strings of pale-red rays coiled around the curved tips of his jeweled earrings— as they seemed to play upon him, their wings incessantly fluttering, while he himself, expert in discerning the nuances of grammar and musical notes, appeared to be singing along.

His hair was bound by a wreath of full-blown *mālatī* flowers, which, like a halo around his moon-like face, resembled a circle of moonlight from his fingernails clinging to him during his playful seizing of a king’s locks;

he appeared as if being personally consecrated by the waters of the confluence at Prayāga, brought together by the mingling of the luster of pearls from his crest-ornaments with the mass of emerald rays, both blending into a dark, turbid stream.

With their crescent-moon-shaped foreheads appearing dark blue due to a blackness fashioned by the smudges of thick black agallochum paste dissolved by sweat, as if by the bruises of hundreds of falls at her feet during hundreds of clever and flattering prostrations; and being embraced by shimmering necklaces that rose from their agitated hearts like clusters of surging waves, while their creeper-like eyebrows—tremulous with the playfulness of their graceful movements—seemed to frown with envy.

With long, dark tresses that seemed to threaten Fortune itself, and with fragrant breaths as pervasive as the Malaya breeze acting like snares to draw her toward them; with large, jar-like breasts encircled by rows of variegated *bakula* flowers like precious gems, as if extracting the entire essence of contentment with their own husbands;

and with the rays of the trembling jewels of their necklaces—swaying from the agitation of their heaving bosoms—as if forcibly drawing in and making him enter their hearts by means of those light-emitting ornaments.

With their upturned sprout-like hands, which served as veils for their lotus-faces made lovely by the persistence of yawning, they seemed to restrain their minds that had rushed forth impetuously; with eyes whose corners were contracted by the pollen of ear-flowers scattered by swarms of bees blinded by passion, and which appeared like buds closed from the swoon caused by the strike of the multitude of flowers’ arrows, they moved them skillfully; and, out of mutual rivalry, they cast glances that surpassed the graceful play of one another’s arching brows.
Striking [him] as if with side-glances that were blue lotuses for their ears; drinking him, as it were, with eyes whose lashes were slowed by the essence of the pleasure of unblinking gazing;

bearing him reflected in the surface of their tender cheeks as if he had been swallowed; bringing forth, through playful smiles devoid of cause, moonrises for the aid of Love; and with the twisting of their limbs and the interlocking of their upturned hands like braids.

His good fortune was being plundered on all sides by courtesans who, in their rage, seemed to break the useless bows of Kāma under the guise of the mass of nail-lustre being coiled like bracelets upon their fingers that were cracking and becoming resonant;

he was laughing at a female foot-grasper whose lotus-feet had slipped from her sprout-like hands— which were trembling and perspiring from his touch— and was playfully striking her gently on the head with the plectrum.
With his hand constantly holding the plectrum, he seemed to be instructing even the Goddess Śrī in the art of the lute, as if she were his own beloved;
he was "without affection" because of his riches,
and "unworthy of refuge" because of his faults.
He was thought to be "fond of suppression" by the senses,
"difficult to approach" by the Kali age, and "devoid of flavor" by vices.
He was branded as "timid" by infamy,
as "one whose mental state is difficult to grasp" by the God of Love, and as "devoted to women" by Sarasvatī.
He was called a eunuch by the wives of others,
a wooden ascetic by the mendicants, and a rogue by the courtesans.
He is regarded as a friend by his allies, as a servant by the Brahmins, and as a good comrade by the warriors of his enemies.
Even though he was one, he was perceived as many:
Śantanu, the commander of a great army,
and Bhīṣma, who shone with the splendor of victory.
From Droṇa he learned the art of the light arrow;
from the son of the Preceptor, unerring aim;
and from Karṇa, devotion to friends.
He was more patient than Yudhiṣṭhira,
possessed of the strength of many tens of thousands of elephants greater than Bhīma,
and more capable of crossing the Mahābhārata war than Dhanañjaya.
Like the cause of the Kṛta age,
like the seed of the creation of the wise,
like the island of origin for pride;
Like a single dwelling for compassion,
like a neighbor to the Supreme Person,
and like a mountain of ore for valor;
It was like a concert hall for all the sciences of Sarasvatī,
like a second day for the churning of the nectar for the emergence of Lakṣmī,
and like a display of strength for cleverness.
Like a single locus for all states of being, like a complete narration of beauty,
and like the final liberation for the creation of the atoms of form;
It was like an atonement for all evil conduct for the sake of sovereignty,
like a full-scale assault with all forces gathered for Kandarpa,
and like a means for beholding Purandara.
It was like a turning point for righteousness,
like a maiden’s inner apartments for the arts,
like the supreme standard of good fortune, and like the day of the final purificatory bath marking the completion of the creation of all the lords of progeny by the King.
It is profound, serene,
and yet inspires awe.
It was delightful, curiosity-inducing,
and meritorious.
He beheld Harṣa, the Cakravartin.

Upon seeing him, as if both favored and constrained, as if filled with longing and yet satisfied, with his hair standing on end and shedding drops of tears of joy from his face, he reflected from afar with a smile of wonder: "This is that one of noble birth."
One whose name is well-received,
a mass of splendor,
and the sole householder for the field of the four oceans.

The supreme lord, King Harṣa, is the enjoyer of the fruit from the root of Brahmā to the tip of a blade of grass; he is the preeminent champion who has conquered the deeds of all kings beginning with Sakala.
Indeed, by him alone the earth possesses a true king.

His childhood pranks were not like those of Indra, which were hostile toward the bull; his displays of sovereignty were not like those of Paśupati, which caused distress to the people of Dakṣa; his rumors did not portend the destruction of lineages like those of Śatakratu; and his wielding of the rod was not as beloved as that of Yama.
Their treasuries were not like those of Varuṇa, guarded by thousands of sword-wielding crocodiles;
their acquisitions of wealth were not like those of Kubera, which yield no fruit; and their philosophical views were not like those of the Jina, which are devoid of meaningful instruction.
Fortunes, like those of the moon, are not afflicted by many defects;
this sovereignty of his is truly beyond compare.
Moreover, he has suppliants for his generosity.
Treatises for wisdom, speech for poetic talent, and occasions for daring for courage.
They were the outlets for his energy, the gateways to his fame,
the hearts of the people for his affection,
and the reckoning of his multitude of virtues.
The skill of craftsmanship is not sufficient for its scope;
and under this king, even the meditation-bands of ascetics [are made].
The quarrels of kings arise from bookish learning; the disputes of bees stem from giving and taking [nectar];
and the severing of feet occurs among those who follow the *vṛtta* meters.
The conceptualization of four parts for chessmen,
the hatred of brahmins and gurus by serpents, and the deliberations on legal cases by those learned in speech.
Having thus approached, he, wearing his sacred thread over the left shoulder, uttered the word "svasti.

Then, not far to the north of the royal pavilion, an elephant-attendant sang aloud a sweet *aparavaktra* verse: "O young elephant, abandon your restlessness; move with humility, head bowed, observing the vow of discipline.
The heavy goad above you, as fragile as the tip of a lion's claw, will not tolerate your insolence."

But the king, having heard that and seeing him, asked—"Is this Bāṇa?"—as he filled the expanse of the sky with a voice as deep as the roar of a lion dwelling in a mountain cave. When informed by the doorkeeper, "As Your Majesty commands; it is he," the king replied, "I will not see him until I have shown him favor," and turned aside from the stream of blue and white silk.

Waving his hand as if to cast aside a curtain, he turned back the long radiance of his eye—whose tremulous pupil was being drawn toward the corner by his glance—and said to the son of the Mālava king, who sat behind his dearest friend: "This is a great *bhujaṅga*.
When the prince remained silent, having understood the king's words, and the assembly of kings was mute, Bāṇa, after remaining quiet for a moment, addressed him: "O King!"
Like one who has not realized the truth,
like one lacking faith, like one who must be led.
And why do you command thus, as if you were ignorant of the ways of the world? The dispositions and rumors of the world are independent and manifold;
however, those who are great ought to be perceivers of the ultimate truth.
You ought not to regard me otherwise, as if I were someone without distinction.
I am a Brahmin born in the lineage of the Vātsyāyanas, who drink the Soma juice; at the proper time, my initiatory rites, beginning with the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), were duly performed.
The Veda has been correctly recited along with its six limbs; the auxiliary sciences have been studied according to my ability;
and through the taking of a wife, I am now a householder.
What is my "serpentine nature"?
My youth was devoid of such restlessness as does not conflict with the interests of both worlds;
in this matter, I am free from any denial.
By this very act, my heart feels as if it has seized remorse;

but now, while Your Majesty— whose mind is as tranquil as that of a Sugata, who is like Manu in establishing the system of castes and stages of life, and who is like Yama himself wielding the rod of justice— rules the earth garlanded with its entire circuit of islands bounded by the seven oceans, who indeed would act without hesitation?
Even without casting off the mental pretense of one who is bound by every calamity, he will act it out;
let alone those endowed with human form—
by your power, even the bees drink honey as if they were afraid.
Even the ruddy geese seem to feel shame through their excessive devotion to following their beloveds;
even the monkeys dart about as if startled;
and even the flocks of predatory beasts consume their flesh as if moved by compassion.

"In every way, my lord will come to know me for himself in due time; for the natures of the wise are such that they grasp the inner workings of the mind without fail. Having said this, he became silent.
The king also, saying, "We have heard it thus," remained silent as well.
He did not favor him with such kindness as conversation, the offering of a seat, or the like;
rather, as if bathing him with showers of nectar, he expressed his inner affection merely by a glance full of love.
And when the sun, longing for its setting, had descended, he dismissed the circle of courtiers and entered the inner apartments.
Bāṇa also departed as the day, possessing the soft luster of washed yellow orpiment, was fading away;
as the garlanded one (the sun), wearing the peak of the western mountain as a crown, released rays of light resembling clusters of *nicula* blossoms from the sky;
and as the forest regions were being occupied by herds of deer, exceedingly sluggish due to their extreme blindness from the dusk, upon the backs of their most tender gathering-places.

In the garden groves, where the banks of the river were filled with the piteous cries of female ruddy geese agitated by grief; where flocks of chatterbox sparrows sat upon the branches of the dwelling-trees while water-pots for irrigation were being filled at the basins; and where the herd of cows, having returned from their day’s grazing, was suckling its young calves with flowing udders as the thirsty calves drank the rising milk—gradually, as the solar orb, its light turning crimson as if bathed in the flood of the mineral-streams of the western mountain, sank into the drinking-vessel of the evening ocean.
When the followers of Pārāśarya, intent on bowing before the shrines, had their feet purified by water from the Kaṇaṇḍalu river;

when the people devoted to sacrifice were uttering the *vaṣaṭ* call over oblations into the fire whose brilliance was heightened by scattered sacrificial grass and whose hands held the vessels of the sacrifice as pure as they were;

and when the family of owls, the householders of the huts within the hollows of ancient trees, desired to depart from the garden trees whose nests were thick with flocks of doves drowsy from sleep and whose monkey populations were distracted by the presence of monkeys.
When the mass of stars, vast as a collection of water-drops scattered by the evening prayers of thousands of sages, made the expanse of the sky uneven;

when the crest-lock of the Night-tribeswoman resting upon the firmament was as dark as the throat of Śiva; and when the twilight darkness descended, devouring all but a remnant of light, like a young girl; [The passage continues with the description of the moon's rise.]
As the streaks of lamp-light flickered like the branches of the sun’s rays entering a fire after emerging from the threatening darkness;
as the city gates seemed to announce their closure by the clattering of their folding panels;
and as the children, seeking to have their hair braided, listened to the stories told by an old woman who was enjoying the pleasure of her rest; ... [the night] passed.

When the most terrifying onset of night was expanding—a darkness as soiled by the soot of aging buffaloes that caused the *puṇyajanas* (demons) to wake up; when the fish-bannered god (Kāma), whose strung bow resounded, was incessantly raining down a shower of arrows that robbed the intellect of the entire world;
and when the servant class was donning their ornaments, looking beautiful at the start of their amorous preparations and echoing with the clever talk of procuresses.
While the women— whose hips were noisy with the mass of girdle-strings being fastened by the *sairandhrīs*—
and the *abhisārikās*, who wander through the streets of the courtesans' quarters and have no other kinsmen than their lovers, were setting out;
and while the sweet chatter of the female cranes resting in the ponds, rendered dull by the tinkling of anklets, was becoming sparse.

When the cry of the cranes, long-drawn out as it was by sleep, seemed to melt the hearts of those separated from their lovers, and when the clusters of lamps were scattered throughout the world like a multitude of sprouts of the seed of the coming day, he went to his dwelling place.
And he thought to himself: "King Harṣa is indeed exceedingly kind."
Since he feels affection for me even in his mind, though provoked by the scandal arising from such childish fickleness of character, it must be that I have not become an object of his aversion;
for had I been so, he would not show favor by looking at me.
Rather, he desires to regard me as possessing virtue.
For masters indeed teach discipline to those who are to be supported even without words, by means of providing appropriate conduct.
Moreover, shame on me, whose mind is blinded by my own faults and tormented by neglect, thinking one thing and another about this king who possesses such great virtues!
In every way, I shall act accordingly.

Having determined, "He will recognize me as I am at the proper time," he departed from the camp the following day and stayed in the houses of his friends and kinsmen until the lord of the earth, having himself grasped the true nature of the matter, became gracious toward him;
and then he entered the royal palace once again.
In a very few days, the king, being exceedingly pleased, raised him to the highest pinnacle of honor, affection, confidence, wealth, jesting, and influence born of his favor.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Audience with the King," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the great poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
